So, it being calm weather, they broke out deeper and deeper, disturbing the slumbers of the huge ground-tier butts; and from that black midnight sending those gigantic moles into the daylight above. Top-heavy was the ship as a dinnerless student with all Aristotle in his head. Well was it that the Typhoons did not visit them then.
Now, at this time it was that my poor pagan companion, and fast bosom-friend, Queequeg, was seized with a fever, which brought him nigh to his endless end.

Be it said, that in this vocation of whaling, sinecures are unknown; dignity and danger go hand in hand; till you get to be Captain, the higher you rise the harder you toil. So with poor Queequeg, who, as harpooneer, must not only face all the rage of the living whale, but—as we have elsewhere seen—mount his dead back in a rolling sea; and finally descend into the gloom of the hold, and bitterly sweating all day in that subterraneous confinement, resolutely manhandle the clumsiest casks and see to their stowage. To be short, among whalemen, the harpooneers are the holders, so called.

Poor Queequeg! when the ship was about half disembowelled, you should have stooped over the hatchway, and peered down upon him there; where, stripped to his woollen drawers, the tattooed savage was crawling about amid that dampness and slime, like a green spotted lizard at the bottom of a well. And a well, or an ice-house, it somehow proved to him, poor pagan; where, strange to say, for all the heat of his sweatings, he caught a terrible chill which lapsed into a fever; and at last, after some days’ suffering, laid him in his hammock, close to the very sill of the door of death. How he wasted and wasted away in those few long-lingering days, till there seemed but little left of him but his frame and tattooing. But as all else in him thinned, and his cheek-bones grew sharper, his eyes, nevertheless, seemed growing fuller and fuller; they became of a strange softness of lustre; and mildly but deeply looked out at you there from his sickness, a wondrous testimony to that immortal health in him which could not die, or be weakened. And like circles on the water, which, as they grow fainter, expand; so his eyes seemed rounding and rounding, like the rings of Eternity. An awe that cannot be named would steal over you as you sat by the side of this waning savage, and saw as strange things in his face, as any beheld who were bystanders when Zoroaster died. For whatever is truly wondrous and fearful in man, never yet was put into words or books. And the drawing near of Death, which alike levels all, alike impresses all with a last revelation, which only an author from the dead could adequately tell. So that—let us say it again—no dying Chaldee or Greek had higher and holier thoughts than those, whose mysterious shades you saw creeping over the face of poor Queequeg, as he quietly lay in his swaying hammock, and the rolling sea seemed gently rocking him to his final rest, and the ocean’s invisible flood-tide lifted him higher and higher towards his destined heaven.

Not a man of the crew but gave him up; and, as for Queequeg himself, what he thought of his case was forcibly shown by a curious favour he asked. He called one to him in the grey morning watch, when the day was just breaking, and taking his hand, said that while in Nantucket he had chanced to see certain little canoes of dark wood, like the rich war-wood of his native isle; and upon inquiry, he had learned that all whalemen who died in Nantucket, were laid in those same dark canoes, and that the fancy of being so laid had much pleased him; for it was not unlike the custom of his own race, who, after embalming a dead warrior, stretched him out in his canoe, and so left him to be floated away to the starry archipelagoes; for not only do they believe that the stars are isles, but that far beyond all visible horizons, their own mild, uncontinented seas, interflow with the blue heavens; and so form the white breakers of the milky way. He added, that he shuddered at the thought of being buried in his hammock, according to the usual sea-custom, tossed like something vile to the death-devouring sharks. No: he desired a canoe like those of Nantucket, all the more congenial to him, being a whaleman, that like a whale-boat these coffin-canoes were without a keel; though that involved but uncertain steering, and much lee-way adown the dim ages.

Now, when this strange circumstance was made known aft, the carpenter was at once commanded to do Queequeg’s bidding, whatever it might include. There was some heathenish, coffin-coloured old lumber aboard, which, upon a long previous voyage, had been cut from the aboriginal groves of the Lackaday islands, and from these dark planks the coffin was recommended to be made. No sooner was the carpenter apprised of the order, than taking his rule, he forthwith with all the indifferent promptitude of his character, proceeded into the forecastle and took Queequeg’s measure with great accuracy, regularly chalking Queequeg’s person as he shifted the rule.
“Ah! poor fellow! he’ll have to die now,” ejaculated the Long Island sailor.

Going to his vice-bench, the carpenter for convenience sake and general reference, now transferringly measured on it the exact length the coffin was to be, and then made the transfer permanent by cutting two notches at its extremities. This done, he marshalled the planks and his tools, and to work.
When the last nail was driven, and the lid duly planed and fitted, he lightly shouldered the coffin and went forward with it, inquiring whether they were ready for it yet in that direction.

Overhearing the indignant but half-humorous cries with which the people on deck began to drive the coffin away, Queequeg, to every one’s consternation, commanded that the thing should be instantly brought to him, nor was there any denying him; seeing that, of all mortals, some dying men are the most tyrannical; and certainly, since they will shortly trouble us so little for evermore, the poor fellows ought to be indulged.

Leaning over in his hammock, Queequeg long regarded the coffin with an attentive eye. He then called for his harpoon, had the wooden stock drawn from it, and then had the iron part placed in the coffin along with one of the paddles of his boat. All by his own request, also, biscuits were then ranged round the sides within: a flask of fresh water was placed at the head, and a small bag of woody earth scraped up in the hold at the foot; and a piece of sail-cloth being rolled up for a pillow, Queequeg now entreated to be lifted into his final bed, that he might make trial of its comforts, if any it had. He lay without moving a few minutes, then told one to go to his bag and bring out his little god, Yojo. Then crossing his arms on his breast with Yojo between, he called for the coffin lid (hatch he called it) to be placed over him. The head part turned over with a leather hinge, and there lay Queequeg in his coffin with little but his composed countenance in view. “Rarmai” (it will do; it is easy), he murmured at last, and signed to be replaced in his hammock.
But ere this was done, Pip, who had been slily hovering near by all this while, drew nigh to him where he lay, and with soft sobbings, took him by the hand; in the other, holding his tambourine.

“Poor rover! will ye never have done with all this weary roving? where go ye now? But if the currents carry ye to those sweet Antilles where the beaches are only beat with water-lilies, will ye do one little errand for me? Seek out one Pip, who’s now been missing long: I think he’s in those far Antilles. If ye find him, then comfort him; for he must be very sad; for look! he’s left his tambourine behind;—I found it. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Now, Queequeg, die; and I’ll beat ye your dying march.”

“I have heard,” murmured Starbuck, gazing down the scuttle, “that in violent fevers, men, all ignorance, have talked in ancient tongues; and that when the mystery is probed, it turns out always that in their wholly forgotten childhood those ancient tongues had been really spoken in their hearing by some lofty scholars. So, to my fond faith, poor Pip, in this strange sweetness of his lunacy, brings heavenly vouchers of all our heavenly homes. Where learned he that, but there?—Hark! he speaks again: but more wildly now.”

“Form two and two! Let’s make a General of him! Ho, where’s his harpoon? Lay it across here.—Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! huzza! Oh for a game cock now to sit upon his head and crow! Queequeg dies game!—mind ye that; Queequeg dies game!—take ye good heed of that; Queequeg dies game! I say; game, game, game! but base little Pip, he died a coward; died all a’shiver;—out upon Pip! Hark ye; if ye find Pip, tell all the Antilles he’s a runaway; a coward, a coward, a coward! Tell them he jumped from a whale-boat! I’d never beat my tambourine over base Pip, and hail him General, if he were once more dying here. No, no! shame upon all cowards—shame upon them! Let ’em go drown like Pip, that jumped from a whale-boat. Shame! shame!”
During all this, Queequeg lay with closed eyes, as if in a dream. Pip was led away, and the sick man was replaced in his hammock.

But now that he had apparently made every preparation for death; now that his coffin was proved a good fit, Queequeg suddenly rallied; soon there seemed no need of the carpenter’s box: and thereupon, when some expressed their delighted surprise, he, in substance, said, that the cause of his sudden convalescence was this;—at a critical moment, he had just recalled a little duty ashore, which he was leaving undone; and therefore had changed his mind about dying: he could not die yet, he averred. They asked him, then, whether to live or die was a matter of his own sovereign will and pleasure. He answered, certainly. In a word, it was Queequeg’s conceit, that if a man made up his mind to live, mere sickness could not kill him: nothing but a whale, or a gale, or some violent, ungovernable, unintelligent destroyer of that sort.

Now, there is this noteworthy difference between savage and civilized; that while a sick, civilized man may be six months convalescing, generally speaking, a sick savage is almost half-well again in a day. So, in good time my Queequeg gained strength; and at length after sitting on the windlass for a few indolent days (but eating with a vigorous appetite) he suddenly leaped to his feet, threw out his arms and legs, gave himself a good stretching, yawned a little bit, and then springing into the head of his hoisted boat, and poising a harpoon, pronounced himself fit for a fight.

With a wild whimsiness, he now used his coffin for a sea-chest; and emptying into it his canvas bag of clothes, set them in order there. Many spare hours he spent, in carving the lid with all manner of grotesque figures and drawings; and it seemed that hereby he was striving, in his rude way, to copy parts of the twisted tattooing on his body. And this tattooing had been the work of a departed prophet and seer of his island, who, by those hieroglyphic marks, had written out on his body a complete theory of the heavens and the earth, and a mystical treatise on the art of attaining truth; so that Queequeg in his own proper person was a riddle to unfold; a wondrous work in one volume; but whose mysteries not even himself could read, though his own live heart beat against them; and these mysteries were therefore destined in the end to moulder away with the living parchment whereon they were inscribed, and so be unsolved to the last. And this thought it must have been which suggested to Ahab that wild exclamation of his, when one morning turning away from surveying poor Queequeg—“Oh, devilish tantalization of the gods!”

Then he asked for his harpoon, had the wooden shaft taken out of it, and had the iron part laid in the coffin together with one of the paddles from his boat. Next, again at his own request, biscuits were lined up around the inside walls; a flask of fresh water was set at the head, and at the foot a small bag of woody earth scraped up from the hold. A piece of sailcloth was rolled up for a pillow, and then Queequeg begged to be lifted into his final bed so that he could test how comfortable it was, if it was comfortable at all. He lay still for a few minutes, then told someone to go to his bag and bring out his little god, Yojo. Then he crossed his arms on his chest with Yojo between them and asked for the coffin lid (he called it the hatch) to be put over him. The head section folded back on a leather hinge, and there lay Queequeg in his coffin with hardly anything showing but his calm face. "Rarmai" (it will do; it is easy), he murmured at last, and signaled to be put back in his hammock.
But before this was done, Pip, who had been slyly hovering nearby all this while, came close to him where he lay and, with soft sobs, took him by the hand, holding his tambourine in the other.

"Poor rover! Will you never be done with all this weary roving? Where are you going now? But if the currents carry you to those sweet Antilles where the beaches are beaten only by water-lilies, will you do one little errand for me? Seek out one Pip, who's been missing a long time now: I think he's in those far Antilles. If you find him, then comfort him, for he must be very sad; for look! he's left his tambourine behind — I found it. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Now, Queequeg, die; and I'll beat you your dying march."

"I have heard," murmured Starbuck, gazing down the scuttle, "that in violent fevers men wholly without learning have talked in ancient languages; and that when the mystery is looked into, it always turns out that in their wholly forgotten childhood those ancient languages had really been spoken in their hearing by some lofty scholars. So, in my fond faith, poor Pip, in this strange sweetness of his lunacy, brings heavenly vouchers of all our heavenly homes. Where did he learn that, if not there? — Listen! He's speaking again: but more wildly now."

"Form up two by two! Let's make a General of him! Ho, where's his harpoon? Lay it across here. — Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Hurrah! Oh, for a gamecock now to sit on his head and crow! Queequeg dies game! — mind you that; Queequeg dies game! — take good note of that; Queequeg dies game! I say; game, game, game! But base little Pip, he died a coward; died all a-shiver — shame on Pip! Listen; if you find Pip, tell all the Antilles he's a runaway; a coward, a coward, a coward! Tell them he jumped from a whaleboat! I'd never beat my tambourine over base Pip, and hail him General, if he were dying here once more. No, no! Shame on all cowards — shame on them! Let them go drown like Pip, who jumped from a whaleboat. Shame! Shame!"
Through all of this Queequeg lay with his eyes shut, as if he were dreaming. Pip was led away, and the sick man was put back in his hammock.

But now that he had apparently made every preparation for death, now that his coffin had proved a good fit, Queequeg suddenly rallied; soon there seemed no need for the carpenter's box. And then, when some expressed their delighted surprise, he said, in substance, that the cause of his sudden recovery was this: at a critical moment he had just remembered a little duty ashore that he was leaving undone, and so had changed his mind about dying; he could not die yet, he declared. They asked him, then, whether living or dying was a matter of his own sovereign will and pleasure. He answered, certainly. In a word, it was Queequeg's notion that if a man made up his mind to live, mere sickness could not kill him: nothing but a whale, or a gale, or some violent, ungovernable, unintelligent destroyer of that sort.

Now, there is this noteworthy difference between savage and civilized: while a sick civilized man may take six months to recover, generally speaking a sick savage is almost half-well again in a day. So in good time my Queequeg gained strength; and at length, after sitting on the windlass for a few idle days (but eating with a vigorous appetite), he suddenly leaped to his feet, threw out his arms and legs, gave himself a good stretch, yawned a little, and then, springing into the head of his hoisted boat and poising a harpoon, declared himself fit for a fight.

With a wild whimsicality, he now used his coffin as a sea-chest; and emptying his canvas bag of clothes into it, he set them in order there. He spent many spare hours carving the lid with all kinds of grotesque figures and drawings; and it seemed that in this way he was trying, in his rough fashion, to copy parts of the twisted tattooing on his body. And this tattooing had been the work of a departed prophet and seer of his island, who, by those hieroglyphic marks, had written out on his body a complete theory of the heavens and the earth, and a mystical treatise on the art of attaining truth; so that Queequeg in his own proper person was a riddle to unfold, a wondrous work in one volume, but one whose mysteries not even he himself could read, though his own living heart beat against them; and these mysteries were therefore destined in the end to molder away with the living parchment on which they were inscribed, and so remain unsolved to the last. And it must have been this thought that prompted Ahab's wild exclamation when, one morning, he turned away from surveying poor Queequeg — "Oh, devilish tantalization of the gods!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 110 — Queequeg i sin kiste
paragraphs: Da de søgte efter lækagen, fandt de ud af, at de tønder, der senest var blevet firet ned i lasten, var helt tætte, og at lækagen måtte være længere nede. Da vejret var roligt, tømte de derfor dybere og dybere og forstyrrede de store bundlags-tønders søvn, så de enorme muldvarpe kom op fra deres sorte midnat til dagslyset ovenfor. De kom så dybt ned, og de nederste store tønder så så gamle, tærede og tangbevoksede ud, at man næsten forventede at finde en muggen hjørnestenstønde med mønter fra kaptajn Noah sammen med afskrifter af de opslåede plakater, som forgæves havde advaret den forblindede gamle verden om syndfloden. Den ene store vandtønde efter den anden, og brød og oksekød også, og bundter af tøndestave (stave i bundter, til at lave tønder af) og jernbundter med tøndebånd blev hejst op, indtil dækkene til sidst var så fyldt op, at det var svært at komme rundt på dem. Det hule skrog gav genlyd under fødderne, som om man gik hen over tomme katakomber, og det slingrede og rullede i havet som en demijohn, der kun har luft til last. Skibet var lige så toptungt som en studerende uden middag med hele Aristoteles i hovedet. Det var et held, at tyfonerne ikke kom forbi dem dengang.
Netop på dette tidspunkt blev min stakkels hedenske følgesvend og nære hjertensven Queequeg grebet af en feber, som bragte ham tæt på hans endeløse ende.

Lad det være sagt, at i hvalfangerarbejdet kender man ikke til dovne embeder. Værdighed og fare går hånd i hånd, og indtil man bliver kaptajn, slider man mere, jo højere man stiger. Sådan gik det den stakkels Queequeg, som, som harpunerer, ikke blot måtte se den levende hvals hele raseri i øjnene, men — som vi har set andetsteds — også stige op på dens døde ryg i en høj sø. Og til sidst måtte han gå ned i lastens mørke og svede sig igennem hele dagen i det underjordiske fangenskab, hvor han med fast hånd måtte slæbe rundt på de klodsede tønder og sørge for, at de blev stuvet. Kort sagt er harpunererne blandt hvalfangere dem, man kalder lastemændene.

Stakkels Queequeg! Da skibet var næsten halvt tømt for indvolde, skulle man have bøjet sig ind over lugeåbningen og kigget ned på ham dernede, hvor den tatoverede vilde krøb rundt i fugten og slimet, afklædt til sine uldne underbukser, som et grønt plettet firben nede i bunden af en brønd. Og en brønd eller en iskælder viste det sig på en eller anden måde at være for ham, den stakkels hedning. For dernede, mærkeligt nok, fik han trods al sin sveden et frygteligt kuldegys, som blev til feber, og som til sidst efter nogle dages lidelse lagde ham i hans hængekøje, helt tæt ved selve dørtærsklen til dødens rige. Hvordan han tog af og tog af i disse få lange, sløve dage, indtil der næsten kun var hans skelet og hans tatoveringer tilbage af ham! Men mens alt andet ved ham blev tyndere, og hans kindben blev skarpere, syntes hans øjne alligevel at blive fyldigere og fyldigere. De fik en mærkelig blødhed i glansen og så mildt, men dybt ud på en fra hans sygdom, et vidunderligt vidnesbyrd om det udødelige helbred i ham, som ikke kunne dø eller svækkes. Og som ringe på vandet, der bliver større, mens de bliver svagere, syntes hans øjne at runde sig mere og mere, som evighedens ringe. En ærefrygt, der ikke kan navngives, ville liste sig ind over en, når man sad ved siden af denne hendøende vilde og så ting i hans ansigt, lige så underlige som dem, de så, der stod omkring Zoroaster, da han døde. For alt det, der er virkelig vidunderligt og frygteligt i mennesket, er endnu aldrig blevet sat i ord eller bøger. Og dødens nærmen, som jævner alle ens, trykker alle ens med en sidste åbenbaring, som kun en forfatter, der var vendt tilbage fra de døde, ville kunne fortælle ordentligt. Så — lad os sige det igen — ingen døende kaldæer eller græker havde højere og helligere tanker end dem, hvis mystiske skygger man så krybe hen over den stakkels Queequegs ansigt, mens han lå stille i sin gyngende hængekøje, og det rullende hav syntes at vugge ham blidt til hans sidste hvile, og havets usynlige flodbølge løftede ham højere og højere op mod hans bestemte himmel.

Hver mand i besætningen opgav ham som tabt. Og hvad Queequeg selv mente om sin tilstand, viste sig tydeligt i en mærkelig tjeneste, han bad om. Han kaldte en af mændene hen til sig i den grå morgenvagt, lige som dagen brød frem, og tog ham i hånden. Han sagde, at han i Nantucket tilfældigvis havde set nogle små kanoer af mørkt træ, ligesom det rige krigstræ fra hans fødeø, og at han ved at spørge havde fået at vide, at alle hvalfangere, der døde i Nantucket, blev lagt i netop sådanne mørke kanoer. Tanken om at blive lagt til hvile på den måde havde glædet ham meget. For det lignede ikke lidt skikken hos hans eget folk, som efter at have balsameret en død kriger lagde ham udstrakt i hans kano og så lod ham drive væk mod de stjernebesatte øhav. For de tror ikke blot, at stjernerne er øer, men også at deres egne milde, kontinentløse have langt hinsides alle synlige horisonter flyder sammen med den blå himmel og således danner Mælkevejens hvide brydere. Han tilføjede, at han gøs ved tanken om at blive begravet i sin hængekøje, som det var sædvane til søs, og kastet som noget væmmeligt for de dødsslugende hajer. Nej: han ville have en kano som dem i Nantucket. Den var så meget mere behagelig for ham som hvalfanger, fordi disse ligkistekanoer, ligesom en hvalbåd, ikke havde noget køl — selv om det betød usikker styring og masser af afdrift ned gennem de dunkle tidsaldre.

Da denne mærkelige omstændighed blev kendt agterude, fik tømreren straks ordre til at gøre, som Queequeg ønskede, uanset hvad det kunne indebære. Der var noget hedensk, ligkistefarvet gammelt tømmer om bord, som på en lang rejse for nogen tid siden var blevet hugget i de oprindelige lunde på Lackaday-øerne, og man anbefalede, at kisten blev lavet af disse mørke planker. Så snart tømreren havde fået at vide om ordren, tog han sin tommestok og gik med hele sin karakters ligegyldige hurtighed direkte ind i mandskabsrummet og målte Queequeg meget nøjagtigt op. Han mærkede regelmæssigt Queequegs krop med kridt, hver gang han flyttede stokken.
»Ak! Stakkels fyr! Nu må han dø,« udbrød matrosen fra Long Island.

Tømreren gik hen til sin skruestikbænk og målte for nemheds skyld og til almindelig henvisning den nøjagtige længde, kisten skulle have, af på den ved at overføre målet. Så gjorde han mærket varigt ved at skære to hak ved enderne. Da det var gjort, ordnede han planker og værktøj og gik i gang med arbejdet.
Da det sidste søm var slået i, og låget var høvlet og passet ordentligt til, svingede han let kisten op på skulderen og bar den frem og spurgte, om de var klar til den deroppe endnu.

Queequeg overhørte de forargede, halvt spøgende råb, hvormed mændene på dækket begyndte at jage kisten væk, og til alles forfærdelse befalede han, at den straks skulle bringes til ham. Man kunne ikke nægte ham det, for nogle døende mennesker er de mest tyranniske af alle dødelige. Og eftersom de snart vil besvære os så lidt for evigt, bør man helt sikkert give de stakkels fyre deres vilje.

Queequeg lænede sig ud af sin hængekøje og studerede længe kisten nøje. Så bad han om sin harpun, lod træskaftet tage af og lod jerndelen lægge i kisten sammen med en af årerne fra hans båd. Derefter blev der, igen efter hans eget ønske, stillet skibskiks op langs indersiden af væggene. En flaske frisk vand blev sat ved hovedenden og ved fodenden en lille pose med træagtig jord, som var skrabet op fra lasten. Et stykke sejldug blev rullet sammen til pude, og så bad Queequeg om at blive løftet ned i sin sidste seng, for at han kunne prøve, hvor behagelig den var, hvis den overhovedet var behagelig. Han lå stille nogle få minutter og sagde så til en, at han skulle gå hen til hans pose og tage hans lille gud Yojo frem. Så lagde han armene over kors på brystet med Yojo imellem dem og bad om at få kistelåget (han kaldte det lugen) lagt over sig. Hovedstykket klappede tilbage på et hængsel af læder, og dér lå Queequeg i sin kiste med næsten ingenting at se andet end hans rolige ansigt. »Rarmai« (det går an; det er let), mumlede han til sidst og gav tegn til at blive lagt tilbage i sin hængekøje.
Men før det skete, kom Pip, som listigt havde svævet i nærheden hele den tid, hen til ham, hvor han lå, og tog ham med bløde hulk i hånden, mens han holdt sit tamburin i den anden.

»Stakkels vagabond! Bliver du aldrig færdig med al denne trætte vandren? Hvor skal du hen nu? Men hvis strømmene fører dig til de søde Antiller, hvor strandene kun slås af åkander, vil du så gøre et lille ærinde for mig? Opsøg en Pip, som har været væk i meget lang tid nu: Jeg tror, han er på de fjerne Antiller. Hvis du finder ham, så trøst ham, for han må være meget ked af det. For se! Han har glemt sit tamburin — jeg fandt det. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Nu, Queequeg, dø, og jeg skal slå din dødsmarch for dig.«

»Jeg har hørt,« mumlede Starbuck og kiggede ned gennem lugen, »at i voldsomme feberanfald har mennesker uden nogen som helst lærdom talt gamle sprog. Og at når man undersøger mysteriet, viser det sig altid, at de gamle sprog i deres helt glemte barndom virkelig er blevet talt i deres påhør af nogle højtstående lærde. Sådan bringer stakkels Pip, i min naive tro, i den mærkelige sødme i sit vanvid himmelske garantier for alle vores himmelske hjem. Hvor lærte han det, hvis ikke dér? — Hør! Nu taler han igen, men vildere nu.«

»Stil op to og to! Lad os gøre ham til General! Hej, hvor er hans harpun? Læg den hen over her. — Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Hurra! Åh, hvis vi bare havde en kamphane til at sidde på hans hoved og gale! Queequeg dør som en kæmper! — husk det nu; Queequeg dør som en kæmper! — læg godt mærke til det; Queequeg dør som en kæmper! Siger jeg; kæmper, kæmper, kæmper! Men lumpne lille Pip, han døde som en kujon; døde helt rystende — skam over Pip! Hør; hvis du finder Pip, så sig til alle Antillerne, at han er en desertør; en kujon, en kujon, en kujon! Sig til dem, at han sprang fra en hvalbåd! Jeg ville aldrig slå mit tamburin over lumpne Pip og hylde ham som General, hvis han lå her og døde endnu en gang. Nej, nej! Skam over alle kujoner — skam over dem! Lad dem gå hen og drukne som Pip, der sprang fra en hvalbåd. Skam! Skam!«
Gennem alt dette lå Queequeg med lukkede øjne, som om han drømte. Pip blev ført væk, og den syge blev lagt tilbage i sin hængekøje.

Men nu, da han tilsyneladende havde gjort alle forberedelser til døden, og da hans kiste havde vist sig at passe godt, kom Queequeg pludselig til kræfter. Snart syntes der ikke at være brug for tømrerens kasse. Og da nogle udtrykte deres glade overraskelse, sagde han i det væsentlige, at årsagen til hans pludselige helbredelse var denne: I et afgørende øjeblik var han kommet i tanker om en lille pligt på land, som han var ved at lade ugjort, og så havde han ombestemt sig med hensyn til at dø. Han kunne ikke dø endnu, erklærede han. De spurgte ham så, om det at leve eller dø var en sag for hans egen suveræne vilje og behag. Han svarede, at det var det bestemt. Med et ord var det Queequegs opfattelse, at hvis et menneske havde besluttet sig for at leve, kunne en ren sygdom ikke dræbe ham. Kun en hval eller en storm eller en voldelig, uregerlig, ufornuftig ødelægger af den slags kunne.

Der er nu denne bemærkelsesværdige forskel mellem vilde og civiliserede: Mens en syg civiliseret mand kan bruge seks måneder på at komme sig, er en syg vild som regel næsten halvt rask igen på en dag. Så i god tid fik min Queequeg kræfter igen. Og til sidst, efter at have siddet på ankerspillet nogle dage uden at foretage sig noget (men spist med en kraftig appetit), sprang han pludselig på benene, kastede arme og ben ud, strakte sig grundigt, gabte lidt og sprang så op i forstavnen på sin hejste båd, løftede en harpun og erklærede sig klar til kamp.

Med en vild lunefuldhed brugte han nu sin kiste som sømandskiste. Han tømte sin lærredspose med tøj ned i den og lagde det på plads dér. Han brugte mange ledige timer på at skære alle slags groteske figurer og tegninger i låget, og det så ud til, at han på den måde i sin ru stil forsøgte at kopiere dele af den snoede tatovering på sin krop. Og denne tatovering var udført af en afdød profet og seer på hans ø, som med disse hieroglyffer havde skrevet en fuldstændig teori om himlen og jorden og en mystisk afhandling om kunsten at nå sandheden på hans krop. Så Queequeg i egen person var en gåde, der skulle foldes ud, et vidunderligt værk i ét bind, men et hvis mysterier ikke engang han selv kunne læse, selv om hans eget levende hjerte bankede imod dem. Disse mysterier var derfor bestemt til til sidst at smuldre væk sammen med det levende pergament, de var skrevet på, og dermed forblive uløste til det sidste. Og det må have været denne tanke, der fik Ahab til at udbryde vildt, da han en morgen vendte sig bort fra at betragte den stakkels Queequeg — »Åh, gudernes djævelske tantalusplage!«
